newsitem.title: USA: ADM HAS NO COMMENT ON COCOA MERGER RUMORS.
newsitem.headline: ADM HAS NO COMMENT ON COCOA MERGER RUMORS.

text.p: Newly crowned cocoa processing king Archer Daniels Midland Co refused to comment on talk of another cocoa acquisition -- the third this year.

An article in a Chicago newspaper on Monday raised speculation that the U.S.-based commodities giant, which snapped up W.R. Grace & Co's cocoa business and ED&F Man Group PLC's processing operations earlier this year, may be looking to expand further.
"We have no statement at this time," an ADM spokeswoman said. "We are not commenting on the story."

ADM's acquisitions of Grace Cocoa for $430 million and ED&F Man Group for $108 million in the first half of 1997 propelled ADM to the top of the cocoa processing league and shrunk the number of global processors to just three.

Following the two acquisitions, traders estimated ADM's global cocoa bean-grinding capacity would jump to 450,000 tonnes compared with Swiss-French giant Barry-Callebaut's 350,000 tonnes and privately owned U.S. trade house Cargill's 260,000 tonnes.

At the time of the ED&F Man acquisition in late June, ADM Senior Vice President Martin Andreas told Reuters that the company had no immediate plans to buy another cocoa business and would concentrate on integrating Grace and ED&F Man.
But industry sources said another cocoa business purchase would not be entirely surprising given ADM's practice of trying to dominate a market and achieving economies of scale.
"ADM's style is to go in and pay up for market share and then try to be more efficient," said an industry source. "They are willing to take a lump to get market share."
Speculation ADM may be looking for a facility on the U.S. West Coast also fueled acquistion speculation among the cocoa trade.
"Geographically, they are worldwide except for the West Coast," another source said.

Views that ADM may want to beef up its presence on the West Coast spurred talk in June that ADM might be interested in buying Guittard Chocolate Co, a privately owned, family-run chocolate manufacturer based near San Francisco.
Guittard president Gary Guittard denied the rumors in June and continued to deny them on Monday.

"I'm very confident to tell you it is our full intention to keep the Guittard company in full ownership and management," Guittard told Reuters. "We have not talked to -- or considered -- any deal with ADM. In fact, we have been interested in the past in buying companies that they got in the acquisition from Grace."
California-based Ghirardelli Chocolate Co's name has also surfaced in the ADM rumor mill.
"Ghirardelli is owned by an investment group and they don't have a lot of capital, they are stretched a little," noted an industry source.

In 1996, an investment group led by Dallas-based investment firm Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc acquired Ghirardelli from Thomas H. Lee Co. It was the fourth time the company had changed hands since the early 1960s.

Ghirardelli has three business divisions: a retail unit which operates specialty shops, a branded division which produces chocolate bars and other products for retail outlets and a division that sells chocolate chips and cocoa for baking.
But Ghirardelli CEO John Anton also denied the ADM takeover talk.

"ADM is not purchasing Ghirardelli," Anton told Reuters. "I don't know who they're buying. Rumors are flying, but certainly it's not us and we really don't fit with their industrial growth strategy since we're a consumer products company."
Some industry sources also speculated that ADM's next cocoa acquisition may take them outside of the U.S. to manufacturers at origin.
"I would guess it would be outside the U.S. or Europe," said one cocoa dealer. "If they get much larger they may be in for some anti-trust battles."
